title: The Promotion Myth
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: The Promotion Myth challenges the default assumption that career advancement means moving into management. Drawing on data showing 52% of Gen Z workers don't want to become middle managers and 72% prefer skills growth over people management, the author argues that organisations have accidentally built workplaces where the only path to progression requires doing less of the work people love. The piece critiques the lingering belief that success equals becoming someone's boss—a belief the author calls "the promotion myth." Leaders are urged to redefine career conversations away from job titles and toward curiosity, strengths, and personal definitions of fulfillment. Recognition should be extended to expertise, mentoring, and innovation, not just promotions. Flexible paths—co-leadership, project-based leadership, impact-measured success—can keep great people longer. The organisations that thrive will be those offering more than one route to progression.
points: Career advancement has long defaulted to management, but 52% of Gen Z professionals don't want to become middle managers and 72% prefer growing through skills rather than managing people—a signal organisations can no longer ignore.

Dual career pathways (expert, technical, distinguished specialist tracks) allow exceptional individual contributors to grow seniority without entering people management, preserving both talent and motivation.

Performance review questions should shift from 'Where do you see yourself in five years?' to curiosity-based prompts: What gives you energy? What skills do you want to develop? What does success look like for you?
Recognition must broaden beyond promotions—expertise, mentorship, collaboration, and cross-team influence all create significant value even without direct reports.
Organisations with flexible career paths retain their best people longer; when people can grow without becoming someone they're not, they are far more likely to stay.
quotes: That isn't a lack of ambition. It's ambition pointing in a different direction.

Research from recruitment firm Robert Walters found that 52% of Gen Z professionals don't want to become middle managers. Instead, they're more attracted to developing specialist expertise, building portfolio careers, freelancing, creating content or exploring opportunities outside traditional corporate structures.
Somewhere along the way, we decided that success meant becoming someone's boss, even if people were never the thing you wanted to manage.
If we want to attract, engage and retain great people, leadership has to evolve alongside them.
Perhaps that's the promotion myth we've held onto for too long: the belief that the only meaningful way to progress is to become someone else's manager.
The organisations that thrive over the next decade won't be those with the tallest career ladders, but those that offer more than one route to progression.
helping people build careers around their strengths may become one of leadership's most important responsibilities.
